articles.headline: Autism, masking, and building a more inclusive world | Letters
articles.teaser: Readers respond to an article by John Harris on the rise in the number of people labelled autistic over the last 20 yearsJohn Harris’s article addresses all the main issues that are being debated around autism (‘The term is becoming unrecognisable’: have the experts who believed in a single autism spectrum changed their minds?, 1 November). articles.headline: Like the Danes, we need to pay for the society we want | Letters
articles.teaser: Karin Blak responds to an article about children’s homes in crisis and what can be learned from the Danish systemAs a Dane who went through Danish children’s services, and later worked in Sure Start centres as a family therapist in England, I found your article particularly resonant (English children’s homes are in crisis. Does Denmark hold the answers?, 1 November). Adopting similar care here requires two changes: our attitude to paying tax and our electoral system.Denmark’s basic national income-tax rate and average municipal income-tax rate together amount to about 37%, almost twice England’s 20% basic rate. Although allowances and other contributions make this an imperfect comparison, we need to acknowledge Danes’ willingness to pay for the quality of services that underpin a stable society.
articles.originalHeadline: Like the Danes, we need to pay for the society we want | Letters

articles.headline: Huddersfield Town’s most famous fan | Letters
articles.teaser: Readers respond to the death of Patrick StewartIn her enjoyable reminiscences of Patrick Stewart, Marina Sirtis says: “The fact that he supported Huddersfield Town shows you who he is – he didn’t go for Leeds or one of the glamour clubs” (‘We freed Patrick Stewart!’ Star Trek’s Marina Sirtis on breaking in her beloved but very serious co-star, 31 October). Patrick started supporting Huddersfield in 1947. At that time Leeds United (my team) had never won a major trophy, while Huddersfield had won the FA Cup in 1922 and the First Division in 1924, 1925 and 1926 – they were the West Riding’s biggest team.Also, Patrick lived in Mirfield, roughly five miles from Huddersfield but 10 miles from Leeds. In those days, when public transport was the main mode of conveyance to football matches and money was tight, it is only natural that he supported Huddersfield.
articles.originalHeadline: Huddersfield Town’s most famous fan | Letters

articles.headline: Nigel Farage's exit from the Telegraph may be cause for cheer. But there’s a sobering side to this story | Jane Martinson
articles.teaser: The clear-out at the newspaper seems driven less by politics than by a shift towards AI – and journalism will pay the priceNigel Farage has been writing columns for the Daily Telegraph since 2016, most of which have promoted the previously Brexit and now Reform UK party he leads, or accused his rivals of going soft on immigration. For this privilege the paper’s cash-strapped bosses paid him around £4,000 a month, adding up to nearly half a million pounds over the past decade.News broke this week that Farage’s services are no longer required by the Telegraph’s new German owners, Axel Springer, though sources close to Farage say that he resigned. The paper is also reported to be negotiating the exit of Allison Pearson, who has been complimentary of far-right activist Tommy Robinson’s “rough-diamond charisma”, which together have prompted rumours that Springer has called a halt to the paper’s rightwards shift, calling it back to the basics of its Conservative party bible past.Jane Martinson is an academic and Guardian columnist. She is a board member of the Scott Trust, which owns the Guardian Media Group, and writes in a personal capacity Continue reading...

articles.headline: The Guardian view on cocaine and domestic abuse: new links between drugs and crime need investigating | Editorial
articles.teaser: Patterns of drug supply and use are changing and the government’s five-year-old drug strategy must evolve tooA slight drop in the number of drug deaths over a year in England and Wales is the first such news since 2012. Over the past decade, the grim trajectory has been upward; the annual figure of 5,519 has more than doubled since the 1990s. Given this trend, any fall is a relief. But the spike in deaths linked to cocaine, which has overtaken heroin for the first time, as well as evidence uncovered by the Guardian of a link with domestic violence, points to the need for a drugs policy that takes account of changing usage.Nearly six in 10 drug tests on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine in the year to June, while a previous study found that 59% of suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.

articles.headline: No amount of sliding in the polls can shake Kemi Badenoch’s self-belief – or alter her party’s direction | Andy Beckett
articles.teaser: Two years in to her leadership, Badenoch continues to take the Tories ever-rightwards, into comfort-zone Conservatism What happens to a political leader who is too sure of themself? Sometimes, huge confidence is a very useful, self-fulfilling quality: persuading party colleagues, activists, donors and voters that more can be achieved than is usually thought possible. Such utter conviction can keep everyone believing while the actual practicalities of a political project are worked out.Yet when an air of absolute certainty turns out to be overconfidence, the bubble bursts. The politician may be revealed as disastrously complacent and lacking in judgment, having delusions of grandeur, or being fundamentally in denial.

articles.headline: From the US midterms to the hard right in Britain, empathy has become a dirty word in politics | John Harris
articles.teaser: Around the world, virtues such as compassion and kindness are gathering dust, like old hymn books in a long-deserted churchTowards the end of the summer, the Tory-Reform defector Robert Jenrick authored an op-ed piece for the Daily Telegraph about the seemingly impossible economics of rising benefits bills because of mental ill-health. In his capacity as Reform’s Treasury spokesman, his task was to big up its plans to cut 25% of so-called welfare spending by 2030, and thereby tackle what he called the state’s “suicidal empathy”.Straight away, I wondered where this most opportunistic politician had borrowed that phrase from, and instantly found out: a book with the same title, published this year by the Canadian academic Gad Saad, whom the dust jacket describes as having particular expertise in “the use of evolutionary psychology in marketing and consumer behaviour”. Here he is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative in Bloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years, this paper examines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers.
